title: Steve Guerdat wins individual showjumping World Championship gold: ‘I don’t have the words’
content:
The showjumping World Championship is designed to reward not a rider who has one brilliant afternoon, but a combination that can perform over an entire week.

In Aachen, Germany on Sunday, the 2026 title was decided over five rounds: Wednesday’s speed competition, in which time penalties became the first part of the individual score; two rounds of the team competition on Thursday and Friday, whose individual penalties were carried forward; and, finally, Sunday’s two-round individual final. The 25 best combinations after the first three rounds returned on Sunday, with the top 12 from round one advancing to the decisive round two.

By the end, Switzerland’s Steve Guerdat had done what the format demands and what his entire career had led up to.

Riding Dynamix de Belheme, Guerdat won individual gold on 0.86 penalty points, never lowering a rail in the five-round competition. Thibeau Spits of Belgium took silver on 5.60, while Great Britain’s Harry Charles won bronze on 7.17.

For Guerdat, 44, it was the missing piece to a glittering career.

“I don’t have the words,” he said. “I’m just coming down now. My team right deserve this medal as much as I do, and my horse.”

He had begun the week fifth after the speed round, carrying 0.86 penalties. After the next two rounds he climbed into a share of the lead, tied with Germany’s Daniel Deusser. He remained unbeaten through both rounds of Sunday’s final – Daniel eventually finished joint seventh after picking up faults.

The numbers hardly convey what Guerdat had been carrying in his head.

“Yeah, and the World Cup final,” he said when reminded that he had now won the Olympic, European and world titles. “All the titles I wanted when I was a kid.

“I was extremely nervous the whole week because I thought this might be my last shot at it. It’s not all the time that you have a horse like Dynamix in this form.”

Aachen added another layer to the pressure. For Guerdat, the venue has become a personal obsession, he has competed here repeatedly without winning the annual grand prix – one of the Holy Grail’s of showjumping.

“It’s the history of our sport,” he said. “I don’t think it gets any better than winning a World Championship in Aachen.”

There were 40,000 people in the stadium Sunday, a crowd that Guerdat fed off.

“I like to feel it,” he said. “I want to compete where there’s an atmosphere because this is the only thing that makes me want to get up in the morning.”

Dynamix, a 13-year-old mare, had entered the year with little preparation. Guerdat said she had competed only six or seven times the previous year because of his health, when he underwent two major back surgeries for recurring herniated disc issues.

“When I was in Aachen in May, I told my chef d’équipe that I was giving up on Dynamix for the World Championship,” he said. “It was going to be too soon.”

But they built a cautious programme. The mare returned gradually, including a successful Nations Cup performance at Falsterbo. On Sunday, he said, she felt better than ever.

The progression of the three medalists told three very different stories. Guerdat was fifth after round one, joint-first after round three and ultimately first after rounds four and five. Spits began the championship with a time-based score, then picked up four faults in the second round and progressed to produce three successive clears to rise from 15th after the qualifying phase to second at the finish. Charles was 23rd after the first three rounds, carrying 7.17 penalties, then jumped clear in both rounds of the final to climb all the way to bronze.

Spits arrived at the medal ceremony looking unable to believe what had happened after his second round had left him wondering whether the championship had slipped away. Instead, he and Impress-K van’t Kattenheye Z jumped clear three times in succession and moved into silver-medal position.

“I’m buzzing,” the 25-year-old said. “This is not normal. This is what I’ve always dreamed of, what I grew up with, so now to be here myself in this position, it’s unreal.”

Charles’ bronze was perhaps the least predictable medal of the three. He had arrived with LT Holst Freda after only about 10 weeks with the mare and had entered Sunday in 23rd place.

“Never did I dream after the first couple of days an individual medal was possible,” he said. “It’s something I’ve dreamed about since I was a kid.”

For the newly-minted World Champion, Guerdat, all his emotion came bubbling to the surface as the Swiss flag was raised during the national anthem at the medal ceremony: “My life is different now because I have what I wanted,” he said.
